9@9: Giraffes can do math (video, WGN Living)

chunks.text: Scientists have {{found out}} that giraffes can do simple math. [[Researchers]] at the University of Barcelona {{carried out}} a study with four giraffes at a zoo in Spain. They wanted to see [[whether]] the animals could {{work out}} which [[amount]] of food was bigger. The results [[surprised]] many people.

verbs.wrong: To share a fact with the public
verbs.why: You check the mail to find out if a package arrived, and a quick search can find out a restaurant's hours. Scientists at the University of Barcelona found out that giraffes can do simple math.

verbs.correct: To do or perform a task
verbs.why: Doctors carry out tests before a surgery, and a company can carry out a survey to learn what customers want. Researchers at the University of Barcelona carried out a study with four giraffes at a zoo in Spain.

verbs.wrong: To smell the difference in food type
verbs.correct: To find the answer to something
verbs.why: You work out a fair price for a used car, and kids work out how to split candy evenly between friends. The scientists wanted to see if the giraffes could work out which pile of food was bigger.

chunks.text: In the test, the scientists {{set up}} [[clear]] [[containers]] with different numbers of carrot and vegetable pieces. Sometimes they added more pieces, and sometimes they {{took away}} a few. Each time, the giraffes had to {{pick out}} the container with more food. To get the [[reward]], the animals used their long [[tongues]] to reach it.

verbs.why: You set up chairs before a party, and a photographer might set up lights before a shoot. The scientists set up clear containers holding different numbers of carrot and vegetable pieces.

verbs.wrong: To put things in a row
verbs.why: A waiter takes away empty plates at the end of a meal, and a nurse might take away an old bandage. Sometimes the scientists added pieces of food, and sometimes they took away a few.

verbs.wrong: To point at something you want
verbs.correct: To choose one thing from several
verbs.why: You pick out a birthday card at the store, and a shopper can pick out the ripest fruit from a pile. Each time, the giraffes had to pick out the container that held more food to earn a reward.

chunks.text: When the scientists added pieces, the giraffes did [[far better]] than [[luck]] [[alone]] would explain. [[According to the study]], they chose the larger amount about 68 percent of the time. This helped the team {{rule out}} the idea that the animals were only [[guessing]]. The results [[suggest]] giraffes can {{keep track of}} small numbers and can {{tell apart}} large and small amounts of food. However, the animals could not [[solve]] harder tasks, [[such as]] [[subtraction]].

verbs.wrong: To show that an idea is only partly true
verbs.correct: To decide that something is not possible
verbs.why: A mechanic can rule out a battery problem after a quick test, and a doctor might rule out a serious illness with one scan. The strong results helped the team rule out the idea that the giraffes were only guessing.

verbs.wrong: To multiply two numbers together quickly
verbs.correct: To follow the number or progress of something
verbs.why: You keep track of your spending in a small notebook, and a coach keeps track of the score during a close game. The results suggest giraffes can keep track of small numbers of carrots and vegetables too.

verbs.wrong: To choose the thing that you like best
verbs.correct: To see the difference between things
verbs.why: Twins can be hard to tell apart at first glance, and a new driver might struggle to tell apart the brake and the gas pedal. The study suggests giraffes can tell apart large and small amounts of food.

chunks.text: [[For a long time]], people thought that only humans and a few [[clever]] animals, such as [[primates]] and crows, had [[a sense of]] numbers. This new study adds to [[a growing list]] of animals that can count [[in some way]]. The researchers now want to {{carry on}} their work with other zoo animals. They hope it will help us {{figure out}} more about how animal minds work.

verbs.wrong: To repeat the same test one more time
verbs.why: A band can carry on playing even after the lights dim, and a runner might carry on despite heavy rain. The researchers now want to carry on their work by testing other zoo animals too.

You figure out a tricky math problem after some thought, and a mechanic can figure out a strange noise in an engine. Scientists hope this research will help figure out more about how animal minds work.

mainIdea.s: Four giraffes usually chose the container with more food, so it seems they can tell small numbers apart. They could not do harder math, such as subtraction.
mainIdea.why: They picked the larger amount about 68 percent of the time, which is better than guessing. But the study says they could not solve harder tasks such as subtraction.

mainIdea.s: Scientists in Spain tested four zoo giraffes and found they can add and subtract small amounts of food. They say the animals are now as clever as primates.
mainIdea.why: Close, but subtraction was too hard for the giraffes. The study only shows they can tell a larger amount of food from a smaller one.

mainIdea.s: Zoos in Spain have started giving giraffes puzzle feeders to keep their minds busy. Keepers say the animals now eat more slowly and seem much calmer.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a test of whether giraffes can compare amounts of food. It is not about how zoos feed them.

tf.s: Researchers carried on a new study with four giraffes at a zoo in Spain.
tf.why: The researchers carried out (performed) a new study. Carry on means to continue something that is already happening.

tf.s: In the test, the giraffes had to pick out the container that held more food.
tf.why: Each time, the giraffes had to pick out (choose) the container with more food to get the reward.

tf.s: Sometimes the scientists picked out a few pieces of food from the containers.
tf.why: Sometimes the scientists took away (removed) a few pieces. Pick out means to choose one thing from several, not to remove one.

tf.s: Scientists found out that giraffes can do simple math.
tf.why: Researchers at the University of Barcelona found out (discovered) that giraffes can do simple math.

tf.s: The researchers want to carry on their work with other zoo animals.
tf.why: The team wants to carry on (continue) their research to learn more about how animal minds work.

tf.s: This new study shows that giraffes cannot count in any way at all
tf.why: The study suggests giraffes can keep track of small numbers, adding them to the growing list of counting animals.
